conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to make sure you’re getting the emotional support you deserve after having your baby. Today I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply a 10-question check-in that helps us see how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, everything we discuss stays between us unless safety is a concern, and we can pause any time you need. When you’re ready, we’ll go through each question together. Let’s start:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly… it’s been pretty hard. I used to laugh at little things all the time, but lately even the cute things the baby does don’t make me smile the way they should. I’ll see a funny video on my phone and think “that’s cute,” but the laugh just doesn’t come. It feels like there’s a weight sitting on my chest most of the day.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes I can manage a little laugh, but it feels forced… like I’m doing it because I *should*, not because I really feel it. Most of the time the sadness just sits there and blocks anything happy from getting through.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… nothing feels exciting anymore. I used to look forward to little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels flat, like “why bother?” I still do the things because I know I should, but there’s no spark.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

All the time. If he spits up more than usual, I’m sure it’s because I ate the “wrong” thing. When he fights sleep, I keep thinking I must be doing something wrong as a mom. I lie in bed replaying every little hiccup and telling myself a better mother would’ve prevented it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… pretty much every day. My mind keeps racing with “what-ifs” about the baby—what if he stops breathing, what if I drop him, what if I’m not producing enough milk. Most of the time there’s no real reason, but I can’t shut the worry off. I’ll check on him every few minutes even when he’s sleeping peacefully, just to be sure.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart starts racing, I feel shaky, and I’m scared something awful is about to happen, even though I can’t name what. It passes after a bit if I rock the baby or step outside, but those minutes feel endless.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. The laundry, feedings, trying to sleep—it all piles up. I’ll sit on the couch with him in my arms and just feel overwhelmed, like I can’t see how I’ll get through the next hour, let alone the rest of the day.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Um… yeah. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning with worries about the baby and all the ways I’m probably messing up. Some nights I drift off okay, then jolt awake at 2 a.m. and can’t settle again. Other nights I just stare at the ceiling for hours. I’m lucky if I get four broken hours before he needs me again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll be feeding him or folding onesies and suddenly feel like crying for no clear reason. I keep telling myself I should be happy—he’s healthy, I’m lucky—but the sadness just sits there anyway.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a few times this week. Yesterday I couldn’t get him settled and everything just felt like too much; I sat on the nursery floor with tears running down my face while he cried in the crib. Most of the time I try to hold it in, but the tears slip out when I’m alone and overwhelmed.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel low and overwhelmed, but I would never want to hurt myself. My baby needs me, and I want to be here for him.

You've shared that the joy you once found in little moments now feels distant-laughter is forced, daily tasks feel flat, and a persistent gray cloud of sadness follows you. Most days you're overwhelmed, blaming yourself for every hiccup in your baby's care, worrying constantly about his safety, and struggling to sleep because your mind won't quiet. Yet through the tears and panic waves, you remain devoted to your son and determined to stay safe for him.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional, forced laughter and persistent sadness blocking enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely not so much now".</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "all the time" and gives multiple daily examples, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-constant, intrusive worries without real cause, checking baby repeatedly, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes that occur "sometimes," matching the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>"most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling or staying asleep due to racing worries, typical of severe sleep disturbance.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness with tearfulness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes this week when overwhelmed, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 24 falls well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. The pattern of <sym>daily sadness</sym>, <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>concentration difficulties</sym>, and <sym>sleep impairment</sym> aligns closely with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. The presence of frequent <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic symptoms</sym> suggests possible comorbid <med>anxiety disorder</med>. Although she denies self-harm, the severity of mood and anxiety symptoms warrants urgent evaluation to confirm diagnosis and initiate treatment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental health specialist
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment options such as <med>SSRIs</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Engage supportive psychotherapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression)
4. Involve partner/family in safety planning and daily task sharing to improve rest
5. Provide perinatal crisis-line numbers and encourage calls if distress escalates
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (2 wks post-delivery):

• Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia  
• Marked guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
• Daily, intrusive “what-if” worries; nocturnal checking; episodic panic sensations  
• Sleep disruption (initial & middle insomnia) driven by ruminative worry  
• Subjective sense of being overwhelmed / “treading water”  
• Denies self-harm ideation; protective toward infant

Pattern: Consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; no safety concerns voiced.

Screening significance: High likelihood of major postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety disorder; warrants prompt formal evaluation and possible referral to perinatal mental health specialty.
